::: {.resource-intro}
**How to use this module:** Each activity takes about 15–30 minutes,
with optional extensions. Choose the activity that fits your current
work. You don't need to do them in order. Use real material from your
own courses or projects whenever you can, and keep your outputs in a
notebook or project folder so your decisions stay traceable.
:::

**Templates:** [Practice log](templates/practice-log.csv) ·
[Literature search log](templates/literature-search-log.csv) ·
[Synthesis matrix](templates/synthesis-matrix.csv) ·
[Revision plan](templates/revision-plan.csv) ·
[AI use log](templates/ai-use-log.csv)

## Where to start

The skills build on each other across a typical research or writing
project. Use this table to find the activity that matches where you
are now.

| If you are… | Try | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Starting to read for a course or topic | [Compare note-taking approaches](#note-taking) | [Run three search iterations](#literature-search) |
| Looking for sources on a question | [Run three search iterations](#literature-search) | [Audit five citations](#reference-managers) |
| Holding a pile of sources | [Move from a matrix to a paragraph](#literature-synthesis) | [Reverse-outline a draft](#outlining) |
| Struggling to start or keep writing | [A seven-session writing experiment](#writing-habits) | [Reverse-outline a draft](#outlining) |
| Holding a full draft | [Reverse-outline a draft](#outlining) | [Feedback to revision plan](#peer-review) |
| Preparing to share work beyond class | [Translate for two audiences](#science-communication) | [Trace a claim and audit tool use](#research-ethics) |
| About to submit anything | [Ethical AI use: vetting checklist](#ai-checklist) | |

## Compare note-taking approaches {#note-taking}

**Connected guide:** [Note Taking Methods](note-taking.qmd) ·
**Time:** 25–30 minutes · **You'll need:** one short reading (3–6
pages) from any course

**Task:** Practice choosing a method by purpose, and see what different
methods help you notice.

1. **Write your purpose** at the top of a scratch page in one sentence.
2. **Skim once** and fill only two columns: *conceptual* questions and
   *practical* questions. Take no other notes.
3. **Read one section using Cornell notes.** Record in the right
   column, then reduce to cues in the left column.
4. **Read a second section using annotation.** Mark claims (C),
   evidence (E), assumptions (A), and limitations (L), with a margin
   note for every mark.
5. **Recite:** Cover your Cornell notes and answer your cue questions
   from memory. Note what you couldn't recall.
6. **Compare:** What did each method help you notice? Which fit your
   purpose better?

**Suggested record:**

| Section | Purpose | Method | What it helped me notice | What it missed | Recall check (✓ / ✗) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | Cornell | | | |
| | | Annotation | | | |

**Check your work:**

- Quotations, paraphrases, and your own ideas are visibly separate, with
  page numbers.
- Your Cornell summary is in your own words and is three sentences or
  fewer.
- Every annotation mark has a note explaining why you made it.

**Extension:** Turn the same reading into a mind map with labeled
links, then review your Cornell cues again two or three days later
before rereading anything.

**Reflect:** Which practical questions did the reading answer, and
which conceptual questions are still open? Which method will you use
next time for this kind of reading, and why?

## Run three documented search iterations {#literature-search}

**Connected guide:** [Reproducible Literature Searching](literature-search.qmd)
· **Time:** 30 minutes · **You'll need:** access to a library
database, plus the [literature search log](templates/literature-search-log.csv)

**Task:** Build a search deliberately and record each change so that
someone else could rerun it.

1. **Write a focused question** in one sentence and split it into three
   concepts.
2. **List synonyms** for each concept, using two or three relevant
   abstracts to find terms you hadn't thought of.
3. **Write inclusion and exclusion criteria** (date range, study type,
   setting) *before* searching.
4. **Search 1:** Draft the string in a document using OR within concepts
   and AND between them. Run it, then log the exact string, database,
   date, fields, filters, and result count.
5. **Scan the first 20 results.** Note what's on target, what's off, and
   which terms relevant papers use.
6. **Searches 2 and 3:** Change **one element at a time** (add a
   synonym, change a field limit, or adjust a filter). Log each change
   and why you made it.
7. **Screen 10 titles and abstracts** from your best search: include,
   exclude (with a reason), or maybe.

**Suggested record:**

| Date | Database | Exact query | Fields | Filters | Results | Change and reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- Could a classmate rerun every search from your log alone?
- Did each iteration change only one thing?
- Does every exclusion have a recorded reason?

**Extension:** Translate your best string into a second database,
adjusting the syntax. Then chase citations from your strongest source,
both backward through its reference list and forward through "cited
by."

**Reflect:** Which change had the biggest effect, and why? How would
you describe the boundaries of your search in two sentences?

## Audit five citations {#reference-managers}

**Connected guide:** [Reference Managers](reference-managers.qmd) ·
**Time:** 25 minutes · **You'll need:** Zotero (or another reference
manager) with its browser connector and word-processor plugin installed

**Task:** Import sources, verify their records, and check that a
generated bibliography is accurate.

1. **Create a collection** for a current project.
2. **Import five sources** using at least two methods: a database page,
   a DOI, and an ISBN or library catalog entry.
3. **Verify each record against the source itself:** authors, title,
   publication, volume and pages, date, item type, and DOI.
4. **Correct errors** in the library (not in the document), and add one
   or two tags from a short, consistent list.
5. **Add a note** to each item explaining why it matters to your
   project.
6. **Insert all five citations** into a document with the plugin, then
   generate a bibliography in your required style.
7. **Spot-check two entries** against the official style guide.

**Suggested record:**

| Source identifier | Import method | Metadata errors found | Correction made | Tags | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- Every item has a DOI or stable identifier where one exists. Zotero's
  retraction check depends on it.
- No item is the wrong type (for example, a book chapter saved as a
  journal article).
- You didn't edit the bibliography by hand.

**Extension:** Pick one sentence in a draft that cites a source. Reopen
the source and confirm that the cited passage actually supports that
specific claim.

**Reflect:** How many records needed corrections? What does that
suggest about trusting automatic metadata?

## Move from a matrix to a paragraph {#literature-synthesis}

**Connected guide:** [Synthesizing Literature](literature-synthesis.qmd)
· **Time:** 30 minutes (plus reading time) · **You'll need:** three
sources on one shared question, plus the [synthesis
matrix](templates/synthesis-matrix.csv)

**Task:** Compare sources systematically and write one synthesis
paragraph that starts from a claim, not from an author.

1. **Complete one matrix row per source** using the same columns:
   question, methods, setting, findings, limitations, relevance.
2. **Read down the columns.** Find **one agreement** and **one apparent
   disagreement**.
3. **Investigate the disagreement:** Can design, setting, population,
   scale, or measurement explain it?
4. **Write a one-sentence cross-source claim.**
5. **Write the paragraph:** claim → evidence from at least two sources
   → complication → so what.
6. **Underline your claim and circle each author name.** If a circled
   name starts the paragraph, revise.

**Suggested record:**

| Source | Question | Method | Setting | Finding | Limitation | Connection to others |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- The paragraph opens with your observation, not a summary of one study.
- At least two sources appear as evidence.
- Your language matches the strength of the evidence (*suggests* vs.
  *shows*).
- You don't present three studies as the consensus of a whole field.

**Extension:** Add two more sources and a concept column for a theme
that keeps coming up. Do your groupings change?

**Reflect:** What did reading down the columns show you that reading
each source alone did not?

## A seven-session writing experiment {#writing-habits}

**Connected guide:** [Developing a Writing Habit](writing-habits.qmd) ·
**Time:** 10–25 minutes per session, over 1–2 weeks · **You'll need:** a
current writing project of any size, plus the [practice
log](templates/practice-log.csv)

**Task:** Treat your writing routine as an experiment, and gather
evidence about what helps you start and keep going.

1. **Set an if-then plan** for each session: "*If* it's [time/place],
   *then* I'll write for [unit]."
2. **Choose a small unit:** 10–25 minutes, one paragraph, or one
   question answered.
3. **Before each session,** name one purpose: *explore*, *explain*,
   *revise*, or *edit*.
4. **During the session,** stay with that purpose. Note anything else
   for later.
5. **End each session with a restart note:** the next sentence,
   question, or source.
6. **Log each session.** Vary one condition across sessions (place,
   time of day, music or silence, alone or with a group) so you can
   compare.
7. **After seven sessions,** review the log for patterns.

**Suggested record:**

| Date | If-then plan | Purpose | Condition tested | Time or output | What helped | Restart note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- Every session ends with a restart note.
- Missed sessions are logged with the reason, not just skipped.
- At least two conditions were compared.

**Extension:** Join or start a writing session with others for at least
two of the seven sessions, and compare those entries with your solo
sessions.

**Reflect:** Which cue or condition most reliably got you started? What
does a missed session tell you about your schedule, rather than about
your ability?

## Reverse-outline a draft {#outlining}

**Connected guide:** [Outlining and Reverse Outlining](outlining.qmd) ·
**Time:** 20–30 minutes · **You'll need:** 5–8 consecutive paragraphs
from your own draft or an openly available article

**Task:** Map what each paragraph actually does, then propose a better
structure.

1. **Write the draft's thesis or purpose** in one sentence at the top.
2. **Number each paragraph.**
3. **For each paragraph, write two notes:** *Says* (main point, one
   sentence) and *Does* (function: introduces, gives evidence,
   compares, counters, concludes).
4. **Read only the outline**, without the draft. Does it work as an
   argument?
5. **Mark problems:** repetition, gaps, off-thesis paragraphs,
   paragraphs doing two jobs ("and" in the *Does* column), and order
   problems.
6. **Propose a revised order** and a short action for each paragraph:
   keep, move, combine, split, add, or cut.

**Suggested record:**

| ¶ | Says | Does | Evidence used | Supports thesis? | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- *Says* entries describe claims ("evidence that X increased after
  1990"), not just topics ("talks about X").
- Every paragraph has exactly one job, or is marked to split.
- Structural actions are planned before any sentence editing.

**Extension:** Compare your reverse outline with your original plan.
Where they differ, decide which version is stronger and why.

**Reflect:** What problem was invisible in the prose but obvious in the
outline?

## Feedback to revision plan {#peer-review}

**Connected guide:** [Peer Review and Revision](peer-review.qmd) ·
**Time:** 20 minutes to review, 20 minutes to plan · **You'll need:** a
short draft (1–3 pages), a peer, and the [revision
plan](templates/revision-plan.csv)

**Task:** Exchange focused feedback and turn it into a prioritized,
reasoned revision plan.

**As the writer:**

1. Write a short note for your reviewer: your goal, your audience, and
   one place where you're unsure.

**As the reviewer:**

2. Read once without marking.
3. Summarize the main message in two or three sentences.
4. On a second pass, give **one strength**, **two substantive
   comments**, and **one unanswered question**. Tie each to a location
   in the draft and use the *observe → effect → suggest* pattern.

**As the writer, again:**

5. Read all feedback before responding. Sort comments into global vs.
   local and agree / unsure / disagree.
6. Compare the reviewer's summary with your intended message.
7. Write a revision plan with priorities and a reason for each
   decision.

**Suggested record:**

| Priority | Feedback | Location | Decision (accept / adapt / decline) | Planned action | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- Every comment points to a specific place in the draft.
- Global issues are ranked above sentence-level issues.
- Declined suggestions have a reason.

**Extension:** Swap roles and review your partner's draft. Then write
two sentences on what reviewing taught you about your own draft.

**Reflect:** Did the reviewer's summary match your intended message?
If not, what does that gap tell you?

## Translate for two audiences {#science-communication}

**Connected guide:** [Communicating with Non-Expert Audiences](science-communication.qmd)
· **Time:** 30 minutes · **You'll need:** one clearly supported finding
from a source you have read

**Task:** Adapt one finding for two different audiences while keeping
its meaning and limits.

1. **Write the original finding** in one sentence, including its
   conditions and uncertainty (where, when, how sure).
2. **Choose two specific audiences**, for example a community meeting
   and an interdisciplinary research team, or a city council and a
   high school class.
3. **For each audience, fill in a Message Box:** Problem, So what?,
   Solutions, Benefits.
4. **Draft a short version for each** (a 100-word paragraph, a slide, or
   a 60-second spoken explanation), bottom line first.
5. **Check terms:** Replace or define jargon, and watch for words with
   different public meanings (e.g., "significant," "theory,"
   "positive feedback").
6. **Fidelity check:** Compare each version with your original
   sentence. Are the conditions and uncertainty still there?
7. **Test one version** with someone from (or close to) that audience.

**Suggested record:**

| Audience | Goal | So what? (for them) | Key message | Terms changed | Uncertainty kept? | Format |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- Each version leads with meaning, not methods.
- The "so what?" differs between the two audiences.
- Neither version claims more than the evidence supports.

**Extension:** Run both drafts through a jargon checker such as the
De-Jargonizer and revise any flagged terms.

**Reflect:** What did you have to give up for each audience, and what
did you refuse to give up?

## Trace a claim and audit tool use {#research-ethics}

**Connected guide:** [Ethical Research, Writing, and AI Use](research-ethics.qmd)
· **Time:** 25 minutes · **You'll need:** one paragraph and one visual
(figure, image, map, or table) from a current draft

**Task:** Verify where your content came from, whether it is
represented fairly, and whether any tool use is documented.

1. **List every factual claim** in the paragraph.
2. **Trace each claim** to its source. Open the source and confirm it
   says what you claim, at the page you cite.
3. **Check wording:** Mark direct quotes and check paraphrases against
   the original for patchwriting.
4. **Check the visual:** Who created it? What license or permission
   applies? Is it cited? Does it present the data honestly (scales,
   axes, cropping)?
5. **Check data and people:** Does anything identify individuals,
   sensitive locations, or community-controlled information?
6. **Record any tool assistance** (AI, translation, paraphrasing,
   grammar tools), what it did, and what you verified.

**Suggested record:**

| Item | Source / permission | Verified against original? | Risk | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|

**Check your work:**

- Every claim traces to a source you have read.
- The visual has a citation and a reuse right you can name.
- Any tool use is recorded and allowed by the policy for this
  assignment.

**Extension:** Complete the [Ethical AI use: vetting
checklist](#ai-checklist) below for a full assignment.

**Reflect:** Which item was hardest to trace? What note-taking or
citation habit would have made it easier?

## Ethical AI use: vetting checklist {#ai-checklist}

**Connected guide:** [Ethical Research, Writing, and AI Use](research-ethics.qmd)
· **Use:** before you start using an AI tool on an assignment, and
again before you submit · **Template:** [AI use
log](templates/ai-use-log.csv)

AI tools can help with brainstorming, organizing, and editing. They can
also invent sources, misstate findings, and blur whose work is whose.
Use this checklist to make sure any use is **permitted, verified,
transparent, and yours**.

### Before you use a tool

- [ ] I've read the AI policy for **this** course or assignment, or
      asked my instructor. (One course's policy doesn't apply to
      another.)
- [ ] I can say what I'm using the tool **for** (e.g., brainstorming
      search terms, checking grammar) and what I'm **not** using it for.
- [ ] The task still lets me practice the skill the assignment is meant
      to build.
- [ ] I won't enter restricted material: unpublished data, participant
      or personal information, confidential documents, peer-review
      materials, or someone else's work without permission.

### While you use it

- [ ] I'm logging the tool, date, task, and what I kept or changed.
- [ ] I treat output as a draft or suggestion to evaluate, not as a
      source.
- [ ] I don't ask the tool to write sections I'm meant to write myself.

### Before you submit

**Sources and facts**

- [ ] Every source I cite is one I found and opened myself. No
      citations come from AI output without being checked against the
      original.
- [ ] Every factual claim the tool contributed has been checked against
      a reliable primary source.
- [ ] Each citation supports the specific claim it's attached to.

**Authorship and voice**

- [ ] I can explain and defend every part of the submission without the
      tool.
- [ ] The ideas, argument, and analysis are mine, or are attributed to
      their sources.
- [ ] I've reviewed AI-assisted passages for accuracy, bias, and fit
      with my own voice.

**Transparency**

- [ ] I've disclosed AI use where the course requires it, in the
      required format (e.g., a statement or methods note, or a citation
      following my style guide).
- [ ] My AI use log is complete enough to answer "what did you use it
      for, and what did you check?"

**Care and representation**

- [ ] No personal, sensitive, or community-controlled information was
      shared with a tool.
- [ ] Generated images or figures (if allowed) are labeled as generated
      and don't misrepresent real data, people, or places.

**Example disclosure statement:**

> *I used [tool name] on [date(s)] to [task, e.g., suggest alternative
> search terms and check grammar in my final draft]. I did not use it to
> generate sources, analysis, or text for [sections]. I verified all
> suggestions against my own reading, and all citations come from my
> own search.*

**If you can't check a box:** Stop and fix the issue, remove the
AI-assisted material, or ask your instructor before submitting. An
unchecked box is information, not a failure.

## Practice reflection

After any activity, record three things: **what you tried**, **what you
noticed**, and **what you will do next**. Every few weeks, look back
across your practice log:

- Which skills are becoming routine?
- Which steps do you still skip under time pressure?
- Which one habit would most improve your next project?

The goal is a usable process, not a perfect worksheet.
